deep.reconstruction:
Context: in E238 Euler takes a pinned-pinned column of height a and lets the bending stiffness vary along it. He writes the stiffness as Ekk·(s/α)^p, where s = α + βx/a. For several exponents p the equation EI y'' + P y = 0 can be solved in closed form. The first example is p = 4. The fourth example (previous page) is p = 2: the equation is of Euler–Cauchy type, y = √s·sin(v ln s + ζ), and the buckling load is P = (1/4 + π²/ln²(1+β/α))·β²·Ekk/a².

Section XXXIII compares the examples for nearly cylindrical columns. Normalise α = 1, top stiffness Ekk and bottom stiffness m²Ekk, with m close to 1.
- First example (p = 4): (1+β)⁴ = m², so 1+β = √m. The load is P = π² m Ekk/a², i.e. π²·√(EI_top·EI_bottom)/a², the geometric mean of the end stiffnesses.
- Second example (p = 4/3): 1+β = m^{3/2}. Then P = π²(m^{3/2}−1)²/(9(√m−1)²)·Ekk/a², which simplifies to (π²/9)(m+√m+1)²·Ekk/a².
- With m = 1+ω both reduce to P ≈ π²(1+ω)Ekk/a². Euler states that the other examples agree too. This is first-order insensitivity: to O(ω) the load depends only on the mean stiffness (bottom stiffness m² ≈ 1+2ω, so the mean is 1+ω).
- For m not near 1 he keeps the first example as exact for its own profile. He gives the fourth example as P = (m−1)²(1/4 + π²/ln²m)·Ekk/a², with 1+β = m.

Section XXXIV starts on the truncated cone, whose diameter varies linearly from f (top) to h (bottom). If stiffness goes as d⁴, as in a solid circular section, the cone is exactly the first example. The next page then gives P = π²(h²/f²)·Ekk/a². He also considers the alternative hypothesis that stiffness goes as d³. He approximates that case by p = 4 and p = 2 profiles matched to first order at the top. He argues the true value lies between the two results and recommends taking a mean.
errors: No mathematical errors on this page. All three load formulas and the small-ω limits check out: (m−1)/ln m ≈ 1+ω/2, so its square ≈ 1+ω.
Typo on the previous page: l(+β/α) should read l(1+β/α).

The remark that the first example 'demeure dans son entier' needs care. For equal end stiffnesses the p = 2 profile is stiffer in the middle than the p = 4 profile. For example, m = 4 gives about 48.5 versus 39.5 in units of Ekk/a², so the two examples are not comparable as bounds when the end values are matched. Euler only uses the bracketing argument (next page) when the profiles are matched to first order at the top.

ideas.what: Exact buckling load of a pinned column with stiffness proportional to (linear)^4, e.g. a solid truncated cone: P = π²√(EI₁EI₂)/L²
ideas.modern_name: Buckling of tapered (conical) columns; geometric-mean stiffness formula
ideas.usually_credited_to: Euler (E238), and Lagrange 1770–73 on columns of variable section; later in Dinnik and Timoshenko's tables
ideas.where_published: E238, Mém. Acad. Berlin 13 (1757, publ. 1759); conical columns also treated in later Euler column papers (unsure of exact ones)

ideas.what: Stiffness ∝ s²: Euler–Cauchy equation with an oscillatory √s·sin(v ln s) solution and a load formula involving ln(1+β)
All the variable-stiffness solutions agree to first order in the taper: P ≈ π²·(mean stiffness)/a²
ideas.where_published: E238 (this page), as an observation drawn from the examples

ideas.what: Bracketing an unsolvable profile (stiffness ∝ d³) between two solvable ones and averaging
ideas.modern_name: Comparison or monotonicity bounds for eigenvalues (Sturm comparison)

missed.claim: Euler observes empirically that, for small taper, the buckling load depends only on the average stiffness. This is an early instance of the insensitivity behind Rayleigh's quotient, but it is stated without any general principle. It is likely noted, at least implicitly, in Truesdell's commentary, so it is probably not new.
missed.quote: si m = 1+ω, de sorte que ω soit fort petit, on aura P = ππ(1+ω).Ekk/aa : ce même accord se trouve aussi dans les autres exemples
missed.why_it_might_matter_today: Only of historical interest, as a precursor of perturbative and variational eigenvalue estimates.

deep.surprise_reason: The results (tapered-column loads, the geometric-mean formula for the cone, first-order agreement) are correct and in Euler's published paper, which Truesdell and Timoshenko discuss. Nothing here appears absent from the record, though the perturbative observation is a nice early touch.
transcription_corrections: The parameter printed as β in the transcription is a fraktur letter (𝔅/ℭ) in the original, matching the next page's 𝔅.
Previous page: 'l(+β/α)' should be 'l(1+β/α)' (likely a printing or transcription slip).
